title: Language Models and Transformers
subtitle: Word vectors, sequence models, attention, and building a GPT
overview: How large language models work: word vectors, sequence models, attention and the Transformer, ending with a small GPT you build. For HAI research, these mechanics explain why chatbots can be fluent yet wrong, why outputs vary, and what explanations of model behavior can show.

modules.title: Words as vectors
modules.goal: Explain how language models represent words as vectors, why similar words get similar vectors, and what 'predicting the next word' means.
modules.guide: Start with Lee & Trott, then 3Blue1Brown's short overview. Next read Alammar's word2vec essay, then skim Mikolov et al., the original word2vec paper. Key terms: 'vector' (a list of numbers, treated as a point in space); 'embedding' (a learned vector for an item like a word, near related items); 'token' (a word or word piece the model processes); 'language model' (assigns probabilities to the next token).

resources.title: Large language models, explained with a minimum of math and jargon
resources.why: A jargon-free, end-to-end tour of how an LLM works, giving you a mental model for this stage.
resources.focus: Read it all. Note the sections on word vectors, attention as information-sharing, and the feed-forward step.

resources.title: Large Language Models explained briefly
resources.why: A short visual overview of next-word prediction, pretraining, and the extra training that makes a chatbot.
resources.focus: Note that output is a probability distribution over next words, and why responses vary each time.

resources.title: The Illustrated Word2vec
resources.why: Shows step by step how word embeddings are learned from text.
resources.focus: Read the personality-embedding analogy, word-analogy examples, and the skipgram and negative sampling sections.

resources.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
resources.authors: Tomas Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, Jeffrey Dean
resources.why: The original word2vec paper, showing that vector arithmetic captures relationships between words.
resources.focus: Read the abstract, CBOW and Skip-gram architectures, and word-analogy results. Skim the complexity analysis.

quiz.q: Lee & Trott describe the word vectors used in the most powerful version of GPT-3. How big are they?
choices: 3 numbers, like coordinates in space
300 numbers, the same as word2vec
12,288 numbers per word
One number per word in the dictionary
quiz.explain: Lee & Trott note GPT-3's word vectors have 12,288 dimensions, about 20 times more than Google's 2013 word2vec vectors (300). They suggest the extra dimensions act as scratch space for notes about each word's context.

quiz.q: In Lee & Trott's explanation, what happens in the attention step versus the feed-forward step?
choices: Attention lets words exchange information with relevant other words; the feed-forward step processes each word's vector on its own, without exchanging information between words
Attention predicts the next word; the feed-forward step reads the input text
Both steps exchange information between all words equally
Attention removes unimportant words from the input; the feed-forward step adds new words
quiz.explain: They describe words 'looking around' for relevant context in the attention step and each word 'thinking about' what it gathered in the feed-forward step, where no information is exchanged between words.

quiz.q: In word2vec embeddings, the vector for 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' lands closest to 'queen'. What does this show?
choices: The model was explicitly programmed with a list of gender relationships
Relationships between words can correspond to consistent directions in the embedding space, learned only from patterns of word co-occurrence
Word vectors are random, and this is a coincidence
The model understands royalty the way humans do
quiz.explain: Mikolov et al. and Alammar show that offsets between vectors capture relationships learned from text alone. The last option overclaims — the result shows statistical regularities, not human-like understanding.

quiz.q: What is the training task in skipgram, as Alammar explains it?
choices: Translate a word into another language
Classify whole documents by topic
Generate a dictionary definition for each word
Given a word, predict the words that appear near it in a window of text
quiz.explain: Skipgram uses each word to predict its neighbors within a context window; the embeddings that make this prediction work are the useful by-product. Negative sampling makes this efficient by contrasting real neighbors with random words.

quiz.q: Why can a chatbot give a different answer to the exact same prompt, according to 3Blue1Brown's overview?
choices: Because it searches the internet for a new answer every time
Because its parameters are retrained after every message
Because the model outputs a probability for every possible next word, and the chatbot samples from that distribution, sometimes picking less likely words
Because a human reviewer rewrites some responses
quiz.explain: The model produces a probability distribution over next words; sampling (rather than always picking the top word) makes text more natural but means outputs vary run to run. This matters for HAI studies that compare responses across participants.

quiz.q: According to 3Blue1Brown's overview, how does a pretrained next-word predictor become a helpful chatbot assistant?
choices: It needs no further training; pretraining alone makes it an assistant
Through additional training, including reinforcement learning with human feedback, where people flag unhelpful or problematic responses
By writing a long list of rules for every possible question
By deleting all its training data
quiz.explain: The video distinguishes pretraining on vast amounts of text from further training such as RLHF that shapes the model's behavior as an assistant. Stage 4 covers this in depth.

modules.title: Sequences and attention
modules.goal: Explain how recurrent networks process sequences, why compressing a sentence into one vector is a bottleneck, and how attention fixes it.
modules.guide: Read Olah's LSTM essay, then Alammar's seq2seq essay. Skim Sutskever et al. (sequence-to-sequence) and Bahdanau et al. (attention). Weng's survey is optional. Key terms: 'RNN' (reads a sequence step by step, passing a 'hidden state' summary forward); 'LSTM' (an RNN with gates to keep or forget); 'encoder'/'decoder' (turns input into vectors / generates output from them); 'softmax' (turns scores into probabilities summing to 1); 'attention' (a relevance-weighted average of vectors).

resources.title: Understanding LSTM Networks
resources.why: A visual explanation of RNNs and LSTMs, the main sequence models before Transformers.
resources.focus: Read the RNN, long-term dependency, and step-by-step LSTM sections. Skim the variants at the end.

resources.title: Visualizing A Neural Machine Translation Model (Mechanics of Seq2seq Models With Attention)
resources.why: Animates the encoder-decoder architecture and shows what attention adds, bridging to the Transformer.
resources.focus: Read it all; pause on the context-vector and attention-scoring animations.

resources.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
resources.authors: Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, Quoc V. Le
resources.why: Showed an encoder-decoder network could learn translation end to end, establishing sequence-to-sequence learning.
resources.focus: Read the abstract, introduction, and model section; note the trick of reversing the source sentence.

resources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
resources.authors: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio
resources.why: Introduced attention for translation; its alignment plots were an early, later debated, form of model explanation.
resources.focus: Read the abstract, introduction, and the alignment (attention) model section. Look at the alignment figures.

resources.title: Attention? Attention!
resources.why: A clear survey of attention variants with consistent notation, useful as a reference.
resources.focus: Read the opening on why attention was invented and the summary of mechanisms; skim the rest.

quiz.q: According to Olah, what problem do plain RNNs have that LSTMs were designed to fix?
choices: They cannot process sequences at all
In practice they struggle to learn long-term dependencies, where relevant information appeared many steps earlier
They require labeled data for every word
They only work on images
quiz.explain: Olah explains that while RNNs can in theory handle long-term dependencies, in practice they fail to learn them as the gap grows; LSTMs add a cell state and gates to make long-range information easier to keep.

quiz.q: In an LSTM, what does the forget gate output, and what does it control?
choices: A number between 0 and 1 for each value in the cell state, controlling how much of it to keep
A single on/off switch that resets the whole network
The next word in the output
The learning rate for the current step
quiz.explain: Olah describes the forget gate as a sigmoid layer that outputs values between 0 ('completely get rid of this') and 1 ('completely keep this') for each number in the cell state.

quiz.q: Alammar describes a problem with the basic encoder-decoder model. What is it?
choices: The decoder is too large to train
The encoder only reads the first word
The model cannot generate output longer than one word
The whole input sentence must be squeezed into one fixed context vector, which becomes a bottleneck for long sentences
quiz.explain: The single context vector turned out to be a bottleneck, making long sentences hard. Attention addresses it by letting the decoder look at all the encoder's hidden states rather than only the last one.

quiz.q: How does an attention decoder decide which parts of the input to focus on at each output step?
choices: It always focuses on the input word in the same position
A human annotator marks the relevant words
It scores each encoder hidden state, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes a weighted sum of the hidden states
It randomly selects one input word
quiz.explain: Alammar walks through scoring each encoder hidden state, applying softmax, and summing the weighted states into a context vector specific to that decoding step.

quiz.q: Sutskever et al. found a simple trick that substantially improved their LSTM translation model. What was it?
choices: Translating one letter at a time
Reversing the order of the words in the source sentence
Removing all punctuation
Training only on very short sentences
quiz.explain: Reversing the source sentence introduced many short-term dependencies between source and target words, which made optimization easier. The authors report it as one of their key findings.

quiz.q: Bahdanau et al.'s attention produces 'alignment' weights that can be drawn as a heat map between source and target words. An HAI researcher wants to show these to users as explanations. What is a reasonable caution?
choices: Attention weights are random and carry no information
Attention weights are guaranteed to be a complete and faithful explanation of the model's decision
Users always prefer no explanation
The weights show where the model attended when producing each word, which is suggestive but not necessarily a full account of why it produced that output
quiz.explain: Bahdanau et al. present alignments as an intuitive view of what the model attends to, and they often match human intuitions about translation. Whether attention weights are faithful explanations is a separate question — one that later explainability research debates.

modules.title: The Transformer
modules.goal: Explain the Transformer's main parts (embeddings, self-attention with queries, keys and values, multi-head attention, feed-forward layers) and why it replaced RNNs.
modules.guide: Watch the two 3Blue1Brown chapters, then read Alammar's Illustrated Transformer, then Vaswani et al. (Section 3). Optional: the chapter 7 video on where facts are stored. Key terms: 'self-attention' (tokens attend to others in their sequence); 'query', 'key', 'value' (what a token seeks, offers, passes on); 'multi-head attention' (parallel attention operations); 'positional encoding' (adds word order); 'logits' (raw scores before softmax); 'temperature' (rescales logits to tune sampling randomness).

resources.title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs | Deep Learning Chapter 5
resources.why: Traces data flow in a GPT-style model: tokens to embeddings, through attention and MLPs, to next-token probabilities.
resources.focus: Focus on the embedding matrix, the unembedding step, and softmax with temperature.

resources.title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
resources.why: Visually walks through queries, keys, values and masking, needed to judge claims about what models 'attend to'.
resources.focus: Follow the adjective-noun example for queries and keys, then masking and multiple heads.

resources.title: The Illustrated Transformer
resources.why: The most widely used illustrated guide to the original Transformer.
resources.focus: Read all sections through 'The Decoder Side'; skim the training section.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need
resources.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
resources.why: Introduced the Transformer, the architecture underlying essentially every modern LLM.
resources.focus: Read the abstract, introduction, Section 3 (especially 3.2, attention), and Section 4 (why self-attention). Skim results.

resources.title: How might LLMs store facts | Deep Learning Chapter 7
resources.why: Explores how MLP layers might store facts and introduces superposition, background for later interpretability stages.
resources.focus: Follow the worked example of retrieving a fact and the closing discussion of superposition.

quiz.q: In 3Blue1Brown's chapter 5, what does 'temperature' do when sampling the next token?
choices: It changes the number of layers used
It controls how fast the model runs
It rescales the scores before softmax: higher temperature spreads probability more evenly (more random), lower temperature concentrates it on the top choices
It removes rare tokens from the vocabulary permanently
quiz.explain: Dividing logits by a temperature before softmax flattens (high T) or sharpens (low T) the distribution. At very low temperature the model almost always picks the most likely token.

quiz.q: In self-attention, what roles do the query and key vectors play?
choices: The query encodes what a token is looking for; keys encode what each token offers; their dot product measures how relevant one token is to another
The query stores the token's spelling and the key stores its position
Queries and keys are the final output probabilities
Keys are passwords that prevent tokens from being changed
quiz.explain: 3Blue1Brown's chapter 6 shows each token producing a query and a key; large dot products mean high relevance, and after softmax these become weights for summing the value vectors.

quiz.q: Why do GPT-style models 'mask' attention during training, as explained in chapter 6?
choices: To hide private information in the training data
To make the model smaller
To speed up softmax
So that each token can only attend to earlier tokens, preventing it from seeing the very next tokens it is being trained to predict
quiz.explain: Masking blocks attention to later positions, so the model can't cheat by looking ahead. This lets training predict every position in a sequence at once.

quiz.q: Why do Vaswani et al. divide the query-key dot products by the square root of the key dimension?
choices: To convert the dot products into probabilities
Because for large dimensions the dot products grow large, pushing softmax into regions with extremely small gradients
To make the model use fewer parameters
To encode word position
quiz.explain: The paper explains that large dot products make softmax saturate, giving tiny gradients; scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) counteracts this. Softmax, not the scaling, turns scores into probabilities.

quiz.q: What is a main advantage of the Transformer over recurrent networks, according to Vaswani et al.?
choices: It has no parameters to train
It processes one word at a time, which is more accurate
It dispenses with recurrence, so computation across positions can be parallelized, and any two positions are connected by a constant number of operations
It does not need any training data
quiz.explain: Removing recurrence lets training run in parallel across the sequence and shortens the path between distant positions, making long-range dependencies easier to learn. The paper's Section 4 compares this with recurrent and convolutional layers.

quiz.q: Alammar notes that the Transformer needs positional encodings. What would go wrong without them?
choices: The model would have no information about word order, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look the same to attention
The model could not compute softmax
The vocabulary would be too large
Training would never start
quiz.explain: Self-attention treats its inputs as a set; positional encodings are added to the embeddings to inject information about each token's position in the sequence.

modules.title: Build a GPT
modules.goal: Build and explain a small decoder-only Transformer, including tokenization, and contrast it with encoder models like BERT.
modules.guide: Code along with Karpathy's 'Let's build GPT' (builds on Stage 2's micrograd), using Alammar's Illustrated GPT-2 for diagrams. Then watch the tokenizer video. GPT-2 and BERT papers are optional. Key terms: 'tokenization' (splitting text into vocabulary tokens); 'byte-pair encoding' (BPE, builds the vocabulary by merging frequent symbol pairs); 'decoder-only' (masked self-attention, generating left to right); 'autoregressive' (each token conditioned on all previous ones); 'context window' (max tokens attended at once).

resources.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
resources.why: Writing a GPT yourself demystifies what a language model is, the object HAI researchers study later.
resources.focus: Code along: understand the bigram baseline, the triangular mask, and why scores are scaled before softmax.

resources.title: The Illustrated GPT-2 (Visualizing Transformer Language Models)
resources.why: Diagrams the decoder-only architecture and masked self-attention, and contrasts GPT-2 with BERT.
resources.focus: Read Part 1 and Part 2; Part 3 (beyond language modeling) is optional.

resources.title: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
resources.why: Tokenization explains odd LLM failures (spelling, arithmetic, some languages), useful for interpreting user-study failures.
resources.focus: Watch the opening, the BPE implementation, and the closing on tokenization oddities. Skim the library-specific middle.

resources.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
resources.authors: Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever
resources.why: Showed a next-word predictor could attempt many tasks without task-specific training, the seed of prompting.
resources.focus: Read the abstract, introduction, and Section 2 (approach, WebText dataset). Skim task results.

resources.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
resources.authors: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova
resources.why: The encoder-only counterpart to GPT; the contrast clarifies why chat assistants use decoder-only models.
resources.focus: Read the abstract, introduction, and Section 3 on pre-training (masked language modeling, next sentence prediction).

quiz.q: In 'Let's build GPT', how does Karpathy make sure each position can only use information from earlier positions?
choices: By training on one token at a time with no batching
By deleting future tokens from the dataset
By using a lower-triangular mask so that the attention weights to future positions become zero after softmax
By reversing the input text
quiz.explain: He builds the mask with a lower-triangular matrix, setting future positions to negative infinity before softmax so their weights become zero — the decoder's masked self-attention.

quiz.q: Karpathy starts with a bigram model before adding attention. What is the limitation of a bigram model?
choices: It predicts the next character using only the current character, ignoring all earlier context
It can only generate two characters
It requires labeled data
It uses too much attention
quiz.explain: A bigram model looks up the next-token distribution from the current token alone. Self-attention is added precisely so tokens can gather information from the earlier context.

quiz.q: According to Alammar, what is the key architectural difference between GPT-2 and BERT?
choices: GPT-2 uses convolutions; BERT uses recurrence
GPT-2 is built from Transformer decoder blocks with masked self-attention; BERT uses encoder blocks that can see context on both sides of a word
GPT-2 has no attention; BERT has attention
They are identical except for their training data
quiz.explain: Alammar explains that GPT-2 is auto-regressive and masks future tokens, while BERT gives up auto-regression to incorporate context on both sides — useful for understanding text but not for generating it left to right.

quiz.q: How does byte-pair encoding build a tokenizer's vocabulary, as Karpathy implements it?
choices: By assigning one token to every word in a dictionary
By choosing random substrings
By using only single characters
By starting from bytes and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token
quiz.explain: BPE starts from the raw byte sequence and greedily merges the most common adjacent pair, adding each merge to the vocabulary, until it reaches the target vocabulary size.

quiz.q: A user study finds that an LLM is surprisingly bad at counting the letters in a word. Based on the tokenizer video, what is a likely contributing cause?
choices: The model never saw the word during training
The model sees text as tokens that often span several characters, so individual letters are not directly visible to it
The model's temperature was too low
Counting requires a larger context window
quiz.explain: Karpathy traces many oddities — spelling, simple arithmetic, some non-English text — to tokenization, because the model operates on multi-character tokens rather than individual characters.

quiz.q: What is the central claim of the GPT-2 paper?
choices: A language model trained on a large, diverse text dataset can begin to perform tasks like question answering and translation in a zero-shot setting, without task-specific training
Language models must be fine-tuned separately for each task to work at all
Bidirectional encoders are always better than decoders
Larger models perform worse on all tasks
quiz.explain: Radford et al. trained on WebText and showed zero-shot performance on several tasks that improved with model size. The second option is the prevailing assumption the paper challenges.

quiz.q: BERT is pre-trained with a 'masked language model' objective. What does that involve?
choices: Predicting the next word given only the previous words
Translating sentences between languages
Hiding some tokens in the input and training the model to predict them using context from both sides
Classifying whether a sentence is positive or negative
quiz.explain: Devlin et al. randomly mask a portion of input tokens and predict them from bidirectional context; they also use next sentence prediction. The first option describes GPT-style training.

modules.exercise: Using your Karpathy GPT, generate samples from the same prompt at three temperatures. Then design a small user study: what would you ask participants to judge, how many samples per condition would you show, and what confound would arise if different participants saw different random samples?
